sections.title: The OSI Model — 7 Layers of Networking

content.value: The **OSI Model** is a conceptual framework that describes how data travels from one computer to another across a network. It has 7 layers, each handling a specific job. Think of it like sending a letter: you write it (Application), put it in an envelope (Presentation), address it (Session), give it to the post office (Transport), which routes it through roads (Network), across bridges (Data Link), and along physical wires (Physical).

content.title: OSI Model — 7 Layers
content.value:
graph TB
    L7["Layer 7: Application\nHTTP, HTTPS, DNS, FTP, SSH"] --> L6["Layer 6: Presentation\nSSL/TLS encryption, compression"]
    L6 --> L5["Layer 5: Session\nManages connections (open/close)"]
    L5 --> L4["Layer 4: Transport\nTCP (reliable), UDP (fast)"]
    L4 --> L3["Layer 3: Network\nIP addressing, routing"]
    L3 --> L2["Layer 2: Data Link\nMAC addresses, switches"]
    L2 --> L1["Layer 1: Physical\nCables, fiber optics, Wi-Fi signals"]
    style L7 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style L4 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style L3 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#f59e0b,color:#e2e8f0
    style L1 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#ef4444,color:#e2e8f0
Memory trick for OSI layers (top to bottom): 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing' — Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.

In practice, most DevOps work happens at **Layer 4 (Transport — TCP/UDP)** and **Layer 7 (Application — HTTP/HTTPS)**. Load balancers can operate at either layer: L4 (fast, protocol-agnostic) or L7 (smart, can inspect HTTP headers and paths).

quiz.question: At which OSI layer does HTTP operate?
quiz.explanation: HTTP is an Application Layer (Layer 7) protocol. It defines how web browsers and servers communicate using methods like GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.

sections.title: TCP vs UDP — Reliable vs Fast

content.value: The two main transport protocols are **TCP** and **UDP**. Think of TCP as sending a registered letter — the postal service confirms delivery and resends if lost. UDP is like shouting across a room — fast, but no guarantee the message was heard.

content.title: TCP Three-Way Handshake
content.value:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: SYN (Hey, can we talk?)
    S->>C: SYN-ACK (Sure, I'm ready!)
    C->>S: ACK (Great, let's go!)
    Note over C,S: Connection established ✅
    C->>S: Data transfer begins...
    C->>S: FIN (I'm done)
    S->>C: ACK + FIN (OK, me too)
    C->>S: ACK (Goodbye!)
    Note over C,S: Connection closed 🔒

content.title: TCP vs UDP Comparison
content.value:
Feature          TCP                    UDP
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Connection       Connection-oriented     Connectionless
Reliability      Guaranteed delivery     Best-effort (no guarantee)
Order            Packets arrive in order No ordering guarantee
Speed            Slower (overhead)       Faster (minimal overhead)
Use cases        Web (HTTP), Email,      Video streaming, Gaming,
                 File transfer, SSH      DNS queries, VoIP

Real-world examples: When you load a webpage, TCP ensures every byte arrives correctly. When you watch a YouTube live stream, UDP is used because dropping a few frames is better than pausing to retransmit.

quiz.question: Why would you choose UDP over TCP?
options: UDP is faster because it doesn't wait for delivery confirmation
quiz.explanation: UDP skips the handshake and delivery confirmation overhead, making it faster. This is ideal for real-time applications (video, gaming, DNS) where speed matters more than perfect delivery.

content.value: An **IP address** is like a street address for a device on a network. A **port number** is like an apartment number at that address — it identifies which specific application should receive the data.

content.title: IP Address and Port Concept
content.value:
graph LR
    USER["👤 Browser"] -->|"192.168.1.100:443"| SERVER["🖥️ Web Server"]
    subgraph PORTS ["Server Ports"]
        P80[":80 HTTP"]
        P443[":443 HTTPS"]
        P22[":22 SSH"]
        P5432[":5432 PostgreSQL"]
    end
    SERVER --> PORTS
    style USER fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style SERVER fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Common Port Numbers (Must Know!)
content.value:
Port    Protocol    Description
──────────────────────────────────────
22      SSH         Secure Shell (remote login)
80      HTTP        Web traffic (unencrypted)
443     HTTPS       Web traffic (encrypted)
53      DNS         Domain name resolution
3306    MySQL       MySQL database
5432    PostgreSQL  PostgreSQL database
6379    Redis       Redis cache
27017   MongoDB     MongoDB database
8080    Alt HTTP    Common development port
3000    Dev         Node.js / React dev server

content.title: Network Diagnostic Commands
content.value:
# Check your IP address
ip addr show                    # Linux
ifconfig                        # macOS / older Linux

# Test connectivity
ping google.com                 # Is the server reachable?
ping -c 4 8.8.8.8              # Ping Google DNS 4 times

# Check which ports are open/listening
ss -tlnp                        # Linux: show listening TCP ports
netstat -tlnp                   # Alternative
lsof -i :3000                   # What's using port 3000?

# Trace the route packets take
traceroute google.com           # Show each hop to destination

IPv4 (e.g., 192.168.1.100) has ~4.3 billion addresses — not enough for every device on Earth. IPv6 (e.g., 2001:0db8::1) has 340 undecillion addresses — enough for every grain of sand on Earth to have its own IP!

quiz.question: What port does HTTPS use by default?
quiz.explanation: HTTPS (HTTP Secure) uses port 443 by default. HTTP (unencrypted) uses port 80. SSH uses port 22.

content.value: **DNS** (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names like `google.com` into machine-readable IP addresses like `142.250.80.46`. Without DNS, you'd have to memorize IP addresses for every website — like memorizing phone numbers instead of saving contact names.

content.title: DNS Resolution Process
content.value:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant R as Recursive Resolver
    participant ROOT as Root DNS Server
    participant TLD as .com TLD Server
    participant AUTH as google.com Auth Server
    B->>R: What's the IP of google.com?
    R->>ROOT: Where is .com?
    ROOT->>R: Ask the .com TLD server
    R->>TLD: Where is google.com?
    TLD->>R: Ask google.com's authoritative server
    R->>AUTH: What's the IP of google.com?
    AUTH->>R: 142.250.80.46
    R->>B: 142.250.80.46
    Note over B,R: Result cached for future requests

content.title: DNS Lookup Commands
content.value:
# Look up a domain's IP address
nslookup google.com
dig google.com                   # Detailed DNS query
dig google.com +short            # Just the IP address

# Check which DNS server you're using
cat /etc/resolv.conf

# Common DNS record types:
# A      → Maps domain to IPv4 address
# AAAA   → Maps domain to IPv6 address
# CNAME  → Alias pointing to another domain
# MX     → Mail server for the domain
# TXT    → Text records (used for verification)
# NS     → Nameservers for the domain

dig google.com MX               # Look up mail servers
dig google.com NS                # Look up nameservers

Interview question: 'When you type google.com in a browser, what happens?' Start with DNS resolution → TCP connection → TLS handshake → HTTP request → Server response → Browser renders HTML. This end-to-end understanding impresses interviewers.

quiz.question: What does DNS do?
options: Translates domain names (google.com) into IP addresses (142.250.80.46)
quiz.explanation: DNS is the phone book of the internet. It translates human-friendly domain names into IP addresses that computers use to find each other on the network.

content.value: **HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the language that web browsers and servers use to communicate. **HTTPS** adds TLS encryption on top, making the conversation private — like whispering instead of shouting in a crowded room.

content.title: HTTPS Connection Flow
content.value:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client (Browser)
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: TCP Handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK)
    C->>S: TLS Hello + Supported Ciphers
    S->>C: TLS Hello + Certificate + Public Key
    C->>C: Verify certificate with CA
    C->>S: Encrypted Pre-Master Secret
    Note over C,S: Both derive session key 🔑
    C->>S: GET /api/users (Encrypted)
    S->>C: 200 OK + JSON data (Encrypted)
    Note over C,S: All data is encrypted end-to-end 🔒

content.title: HTTP Status Codes (Must Know!)
content.value:
Code    Meaning                    When You'll See It
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
200     OK                         Successful request
201     Created                    POST created a resource
204     No Content                 DELETE succeeded, no body
301     Moved Permanently          URL permanently changed
302     Found (Redirect)           Temporary redirect
400     Bad Request                Client sent invalid data
401     Unauthorized               Missing authentication
403     Forbidden                  Authenticated but no permission
404     Not Found                  Resource doesn't exist
429     Too Many Requests          Rate limit exceeded
500     Internal Server Error      Server crashed
502     Bad Gateway                Upstream server unavailable
503     Service Unavailable        Server overloaded/maintenance
504     Gateway Timeout            Upstream server too slow

content.title: HTTP Testing with curl
content.value:
# Basic GET request
curl https://api.example.com/users

# See response headers
curl -I https://example.com

# POST JSON data
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name": "Alice", "email": "alice@test.com"}'

# Show full request/response details
curl -v https://example.com

# Follow redirects
curl -L https://short.url/abc
Quick status code groups: 2xx = Success, 3xx = Redirect, 4xx = Client Error (your fault), 5xx = Server Error (server's fault). If you see 5xx in production, check your application logs immediately!

quiz.question: What does HTTP status code 502 mean?
options: The reverse proxy couldn't reach the upstream server
quiz.explanation: 502 Bad Gateway means a proxy or load balancer (like Nginx) tried to forward your request to an upstream application server, but that server was unavailable or returned an invalid response.

content.value: A **Firewall** is a security guard at the door — it decides which network traffic is allowed in and which is blocked. A **Load Balancer** is a traffic director — it distributes incoming requests across multiple servers to prevent any single server from being overwhelmed.

content.title: Load Balancer Architecture
content.value:
graph LR
    U1["👤 User 1"] & U2["👤 User 2"] & U3["👤 User 3"] --> LB["⚖️ Load Balancer"]
    LB -->|"33%"| S1["🖥️ Server 1"]
    LB -->|"33%"| S2["🖥️ Server 2"]
    LB -->|"33%"| S3["🖥️ Server 3"]
    S1 & S2 & S3 --> DB[("🗄️ Database")]
    style LB fill:#1a2332,stroke:#00d4ff,color:#e2e8f0
    style S1 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style S2 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0
    style S3 fill:#1a2332,stroke:#10b981,color:#e2e8f0

content.title: Firewall Commands (iptables / ufw)
content.value:
# UFW (Uncomplicated Firewall) — Ubuntu
sudo ufw status                  # Check firewall status
sudo ufw enable                  # Turn on the firewall
sudo ufw allow 22/tcp            # Allow SSH
sudo ufw allow 80/tcp            # Allow HTTP
sudo ufw allow 443/tcp           # Allow HTTPS
sudo ufw deny 3306/tcp           # Block MySQL from outside
sudo ufw status verbose          # Show all rules

# AWS Security Groups (Cloud Firewall)
# Inbound: Allow 80, 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (public)
# Inbound: Allow 22 from YOUR_IP only
# Inbound: Allow 5432 from VPC CIDR only (internal)

**Load Balancing Algorithms:**

• **Round Robin** — Requests are distributed to servers one by one in order. Simple and fair.
• **Least Connections** — Sends the next request to the server with the fewest active connections.
• **IP Hash** — Routes requests from the same client IP to the same server (useful for sessions).
• **Weighted** — Assigns more traffic to more powerful servers.

Interview question: 'What is the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing?' L4 (Transport Layer) routes based on IP and port — fast but can't inspect content. L7 (Application Layer) routes based on HTTP headers, paths, and cookies — smarter but slightly slower.

quiz.question: What does a load balancer do?
options: Distributes incoming traffic across multiple servers
quiz.explanation: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple backend servers, preventing any single server from being overloaded and improving reliability.
